brief.intro: New to this project type? A mosque (or similar single-volume worship building) is a finishing-led project, not a plant-led one — the MEP scope is comparatively simple, but the programme lives and dies on the quality and lead time of stone, joinery, and dome/minaret construction, and on getting the acoustics right in one large uninterrupted prayer hall. Two functional systems matter more than their size suggests: the public-address/acoustic system, which must be tuned for clear speech across the whole hall, and the ablution (wudu) facilities, which see continuous heavy use. Because ceremonial finishes — marble, calligraphy, carved joinery, dome cladding — are bespoke and slow to fabricate, they, not the MEP, are usually what determines the real critical path.

must_get_right: Bespoke finishes (stone, joinery, dome cladding, calligraphy) are usually the true critical path — order and fabricate them early, don't treat them as a finishing-stage afterthought.
PA/acoustic tuning in the prayer hall needs real time at the end of the programme — it is commissioned, not just installed.
Ablution facilities see continuous heavy use — get the plumbing and drainage design right and test it thoroughly before handover.
The large uninterrupted prayer-hall volume constrains HVAC and access sequencing — plan around it rather than treating it like a normal room.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Specialist stone, joinery and dome/minaret cladding packages are tracked as discrete sub-networks feeding final handover rather than folded into a generic finishes activity.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Structure and MEP rough-in run a standard single-shift week. Specialist stone, joinery and dome trades often run on a fabrication-then-install calendar dictated by workshop lead time rather than by site productivity.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path typically runs stone/cladding & dome-minaret procurement (long fabrication lead) → structure weather-tight → architectural finishes & mihrab/minbar joinery install → PA/acoustic tuning → snagging → handover. MEP is rarely the constraint once the hall is weather-tight; bespoke finishing packages usually are.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design — including calligraphy and ornamental detailing — is frozen before fabrication release; a single finishes contractor or tightly coordinated specialists deliver the ceremonial finishes; authority approvals for assembly occupancy are obtained per phase.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Specialist stone, joinery and dome-cladding trades are scarce and often shared across few available crews. The large single-volume hall constrains scaffold and access sequencing for ceiling and dome work; acoustic tuning needs a quiet, substantially finished hall to be meaningful.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks are bespoke-finish fabrication slippage and design changes to ornamental detailing late in the programme. Schedule contingency is held before finishes install and before PA/acoustic tuning rather than spread across MEP activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for finishing and specialist trades — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
